results.name: recency_last_vs_first_example
results.description: In 2+-example sets, for non-example targets strictly closer in size to the last-shown example than to the first (vs the reverse), yes-rate closer-to-last minus closer-to-first; observed above the null means people's size generalization favours the most recent example, which the span-based size mismatch (identical for every example) cannot produce (below means primacy).

results.name: upward_vs_downward_outside_span
results.description: Over all sets, yes-rate for targets 1-20 above the largest example minus targets 1-20 below the smallest example; observed above the null means people generalize upward (to larger numbers) more than the model's symmetric outside-span size mismatch predicts (below means a stronger downward bias than modelled).

results.name: drift_step_curvature
results.description: (yes-rate in trials 150-299 minus trials 0-149) minus (yes-rate in trials 300+ minus trials 150-299); observed above the null means the session drift toward "yes" is a front-loaded / saturating jump rather than the linear criterion relaxation the model assumes (below means the drift accelerates late).

results.name: singleton_near_minus_far
results.description: For single-example sets, non-identical targets: yes-rate within 10 of the example minus more than 30 away; observed above the null means a lone example yields sharper size generalization than the model's (span-shared) magnitude tuning allows, below means people generalize from a lone example more broadly than modelled.
results.code:
# name: singleton_near_minus_far
# description: For single-example sets, non-identical targets: yes-rate within 10 of the example minus more than 30 away; observed above the null means a lone example yields sharper size generalization than the model's (span-shared) magnitude tuning allows, below means people generalize from a lone example more broadly than modelled.
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~ns.str.contains(",").values
    x = pd.to_numeric(ns.where(single, "0")).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    d = np.abs(t - x)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    a = single & (d >= 1) & (d <= 10)
    b = single & (d > 30)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: set_yes_rate_vs_span_slope
results.description: Across 2+-example sets, OLS slope of each set's overall yes-rate on its span (max-min, per 100); observed below the null means the model's span-filling makes widely spread sets too generous relative to tight ones (people broaden less with span), above means people broaden with span even more than modelled.
results.code:
# name: set_yes_rate_vs_span_slope
# description: Across 2+-example sets, OLS slope of each set's overall yes-rate on its span (max-min, per 100); observed below the null means the model's span-filling makes widely spread sets too generous relative to tight ones (people broaden less with span), above means people broaden with span even more than modelled.
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    g = df["rating"].astype(float).groupby(ns).mean()
    sets = g.index.values
    k = np.array([s.count(",") + 1 for s in sets])
    span = np.array([max(int(v) for v in s.split(",")) - min(int(v) for v in s.split(",")) for s in sets]) / 100.0
    m = k >= 2
    x, yy = span[m], g.values[m]
    if m.sum() < 3 or np.var(x) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.cov(x, yy, bias=True)[0, 1] / np.var(x))

results.name: inside_span_near_vs_far_example
results.description: In 2+-example sets spanning >= 30, among non-example targets strictly inside the span, yes-rate for targets within 5 of the nearest example minus targets more than 12 from every example; observed above the null means people still generalize by distance to individual examples inside the span (gaps are not "filled in" as the model assumes), below means gaps are filled even more uniformly than modelled.
results.code:
# name: inside_span_near_vs_far_example
# description: In 2+-example sets spanning >= 30, among non-example targets strictly inside the span, yes-rate for targets within 5 of the nearest example minus targets more than 12 from every example; observed above the null means people still generalize by distance to individual examples inside the span (gaps are not "filled in" as the model assumes), below means gaps are filled even more uniformly than modelled.
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    sets = ns.unique()
    ex = {s: np.array([int(v) for v in s.split(",")]) for s in sets}
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    near = np.full(len(t), np.nan)
    inside = np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(ns)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        e = ex[s]
        if len(e) < 2 or e.max() - e.min() < 30:
            continue
        m = codes == i
        tt = t[m]
        near[m] = np.abs(tt[:, None] - e[None, :]).min(axis=1)
        inside[m] = (tt > e.min()) & (tt < e.max())
    sel = inside & (near > 0)
    a = sel & (near <= 5)
    b = sel & (near > 12)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: rule_set_inside_span_nonmultiple_yes
results.description: In 2+-example sets whose gcd is >= 3, yes-rate for targets strictly inside the example span that are NOT multiples of the gcd; observed below the null means the model's filled-in span over-endorses rule-violating in-range numbers (people let the multiples rule override size), above means people accept in-range non-multiples even more than modelled.
results.code:
# name: rule_set_inside_span_nonmultiple_yes
# description: In 2+-example sets whose gcd is >= 3, yes-rate for targets strictly inside the example span that are NOT multiples of the gcd; observed below the null means the model's filled-in span over-endorses rule-violating in-range numbers (people let the multiples rule override size), above means people accept in-range non-multiples even more than modelled.
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    sets = ns.unique()
    info = {}
    for s in sets:
        e = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        g = 0
        for v in e:
            g = math.gcd(g, v)
        info[s] = (len(e), g, min(e), max(e))
    k = ns.map({s: v[0] for s, v in info.items()}).values
    g = ns.map({s: v[1] for s, v in info.items()}).values
    lo = ns.map({s: v[2] for s, v in info.items()}).values
    hi = ns.map({s: v[3] for s, v in info.items()}).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    gs = np.where(g >= 3, g, 1)
    sel = (k >= 2) & (g >= 3) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & (t % gs != 0)
    if sel.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[sel].mean())

results.name: outside_span_near_minus_far
results.description: Among targets outside the example span, yes-rate for targets 1-10 beyond the nearest span edge minus targets 25-60 beyond it; observed above the null means people's generalization falls off with distance outside the span more steeply than the model's single magnitude tuning predicts (below means a flatter falloff than modelled).
